definition:
Suffering is the pain, loss, grief, and affliction that fall on human beings in a world that is no longer as God made it. Scripture names every kind: the evil people do to one another, the diseases and disasters that strike without anyone's choosing, the consequences of a person's own sin, the discipline God sends his children, and suffering endured for doing right. The Bible does not offer one theory that explains every case. It gives laments that protest to God's face, narratives that show God at work through evil without calling it good, wisdom books that break the simple link between righteousness and prosperity, and at the center a crucified Messiah who suffers innocently for others. It ends with the promise that God will wipe every tear away. This study traces that witness through the canon. The site's systematic page on the problem of evil sets out the philosophical arguments and the Christian responses at length, and the studies of providence and sovereignty treat how God governs a world that contains evil.

Hebrew has a wide vocabulary. The word ra', with its feminine ra'ah, covers both moral evil and calamity, which is why the BSB renders it “adversity” when Job asks, “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” (Job 2:10) and “calamity” in Isaiah 45:7. The noun 'oni means ‘affliction’ or ‘misery’, and makh'ov means ‘pain’ or ‘sorrow’; God uses both when he tells Moses he has seen the affliction of his people and knows their sufferings (Exodus 3:7), and the second returns when the Servant is called “a man of sorrows” (Isaiah 53:3). Tsarah is ‘distress’, a tight place (Isaiah 63:9). In Greek the verb paschō, ‘to suffer’, and the noun pathēma, ‘suffering’ (Romans 8:18), are used above all of Christ's passion and of those who share it. Thlipsis means ‘pressure’ and so ‘affliction’ or ‘tribulation’ (John 16:33; 2 Corinthians 1:4), and peirasmos means a ‘trial’ or ‘test’, though in other contexts it means ‘temptation’ (James 1:2).
ot:
Genesis opens on a world God calls very good, with no pain in it. Suffering enters with the first sin. God tells the woman, “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth,” and tells the man the ground is cursed and “through toil you will eat of it” (Genesis 3:16-17), where ‘pain’ and ‘toil’ render the same Hebrew word, 'itstsavon. Death follows: “to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). The next chapter brings the first murder, and God says, “The voice of your brother's blood cries out to Me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10): innocent suffering has a voice, and God hears it. Before the flood “the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart” (Genesis 6:6), and the verb for ‘grieved’ comes from the same root as the woman's pain. From the start the Bible presents suffering as a consequence of the fall, not of each person's particular sin, and it presents God as neither indifferent to it nor untouched by it. Joseph's story, treated in the study of providence, shows God working through evil done to Joseph without calling the evil good (Genesis 50:20). In Egypt, when Israel groaned under slavery, “God heard their groaning” and “God saw the Israelites and took notice” (Exodus 2:24-25), and he tells Moses, “I have indeed seen the affliction of My people in Egypt,” and “I am aware of their sufferings” (Exodus 3:7). The exodus begins with God seeing, hearing, and knowing pain.

The covenant at Sinai attached blessings to faithfulness and curses to rebellion (Deuteronomy 28), and Israel's historians and prophets read the destruction of Samaria in 722 BC and of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC as the covenant's curses coming true (2 Kings 17). Deuteronomy also names a suffering that is not punishment but discipline: the wilderness years in which God humbled and tested Israel “so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone” (Deuteronomy 8:3), because “just as a man disciplines his son, so the LORD your God disciplines you” (Deuteronomy 8:5). The canon itself then refuses to let the covenant pattern become a rule that every sufferer deserves what he suffers. Job is the great test. The reader knows from the prologue that Job is blameless and that his losses come from a heavenly contest he never learns of. Job first blesses God, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21), then curses the day of his birth (Job 3:3). His friends sit silent with him for seven days, their wisest act, and then defend a strict retribution: “Who, being innocent, has ever perished?” (Job 4:7). Job protests, demands a hearing, and clings to hope that “my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25). In Job 13:15 the written Hebrew text and the traditional reading differ by one letter: the written form (ketiv) reads ‘not’, suggesting ‘he will slay me; I have no hope’, while the reading the scribes marked for recitation (qere) gives ‘to him’, which the BSB follows: “Though He slay me, I will hope in Him.” When God answers from the whirlwind (Job 38-41), he gives no explanation of Job's suffering. He displays his wisdom and rule over a vast and wild creation, and Job responds, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You” (Job 42:5). Then God tells Eliphaz that the friends “have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (Job 42:7). The man who protested is vindicated; the men who explained are rebuked.

The Psalms give suffering a voice in worship. Laments, prayers of complaint and petition, are the most common single type of psalm in the usual form-critical count. “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1), a psalm that later turns to praise because God “has not despised or detested the torment of the afflicted” (Psalm 22:24). Psalm 44 insists that the nation suffers though it has not forgotten God (Psalm 44:17) and cries, “Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?” (Psalm 44:23). Psalm 73 wrestles with the prosperity of the wicked until the psalmist enters God's sanctuary (Psalm 73:17). Psalm 88 never turns; it ends, “darkness is my closest companion” (Psalm 88:18). Yet the same book says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18), and that God keeps the sufferer's tears in his bottle (Psalm 56:8). Ecclesiastes observes “the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter” (Ecclesiastes 4:1), a righteous man perishing in his righteousness (Ecclesiastes 7:15), and that “time and chance happen to all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11).

The prophets bring suffering into the life of God's servants and of God's own purposes. Jeremiah curses the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). Habakkuk asks, “How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear” (Habakkuk 1:2), and ends resolving to rejoice though the fig tree does not bud (Habakkuk 3:17-18). Lamentations, five poems over the ruins of Jerusalem, holds the city's guilt and its grief together and still says, “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed” and “He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men” (Lamentations 3:22, 33), literally ‘not from his heart’. In Daniel, three young men tell Nebuchadnezzar that God is able to deliver them, “But even if He does not,” they will not serve his gods (Daniel 3:18). Isaiah 63:9 recalls the exodus: “In all their distress, He too was afflicted.” This follows the traditional reading; the written consonants can be read ‘he was no adversary’, and the Septuagint reads them as ‘not an envoy or an angel, but he himself saved them’. Above all Isaiah's Servant, “a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief,” suffers not for his own sin but for others: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:3, 5). Here innocent suffering becomes the means of healing for many. And Isaiah promises a feast at which God “will swallow up death forever” and “wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8).
nt:
Jesus refuses the simple equation of suffering with personal guilt. Asked whether a man born blind suffered for his own sin or his parents', he answers, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him” (John 9:3). Told about Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteen people crushed by the tower of Siloam, he asks whether they were worse sinners than others and answers, “No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish” (Luke 13:3, 5). Disaster is not a verdict on its victims, and it is a summons to everyone. Jesus heals the sick, pronounces blessing on “those who mourn” (Matthew 5:4), and at the grave of Lazarus, though he is about to raise him, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). He also teaches that “the Son of Man must suffer many things” (Mark 8:31), a divine necessity, and calls his followers to take up their cross (Mark 8:34).

The passion is where the Bible's teaching on suffering converges. In Gethsemane Jesus says, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death” and prays that the cup might pass, yet “not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:38-39). On the cross he cries the first line of Psalm 22 in Aramaic, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Mark 15:34), taking the lament of the righteous sufferer onto his own lips. Christians confess that the eternal Son, true God and true man, suffered and died in the flesh, so that God is not a spectator of human pain but has entered it. The risen Jesus explains, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26). Hebrews draws out what this means for sufferers: God made “the author of their salvation perfect through suffering” (Hebrews 2:10), the Son “learned obedience from what He suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), and so “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15). Hebrews also calls believers to endure hardship as the discipline of a Father who trains his children for holiness (Hebrews 12:5-11, quoting Proverbs 3:11-12).

Paul sets suffering inside a story that runs from the cross to the new creation. Believers are heirs with Christ “if indeed we suffer with Him, so that we may also be glorified with Him” (Romans 8:17). “Our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18), yet the whole creation “has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth” and believers “groan inwardly” (Romans 8:22-23), and the Spirit himself intercedes “with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Paul quotes Psalm 44's lament, “we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans 8:36), and then insists that nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love in Christ (Romans 8:38-39). Suffering produces endurance, character, and hope (Romans 5:3-4). The God of all comfort comforts his people in their affliction so that they can comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:3-4). Paul is “hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed” (2 Corinthians 4:8), and he calls his troubles a “light and momentary affliction” only in comparison with “an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). He prayed three times for his thorn in the flesh to be removed; it was not, and he heard, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He wants to know “the fellowship of His sufferings” (Philippians 3:10), and he says that in his flesh he fills up “what is lacking in regard to Christ's afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church” (Colossians 1:24). Interpreters agree this does not mean Christ's atoning work was incomplete; they differ on whether Paul means the afflictions the church must bear before the end, his own share in Christ's sufferings as an apostle, or Christ's continuing suffering in his body.

The other letters speak to churches under pressure. James tells believers to count trials joy because testing produces endurance (James 1:2-3) and holds up “Job's perseverance” and the Lord who “is full of compassion and mercy” (James 5:11). Peter writes to Christians slandered and mistreated for their faith: suffering unjustly while conscious of God is commendable, “because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example” (1 Peter 2:19, 21), and they should not be surprised “at the fiery trial that has come upon you” but rejoice “that you share in the sufferings of Christ” (1 Peter 4:12-13). After they have suffered a little while, God “will Himself restore you” (1 Peter 5:10). Revelation keeps the lament alive to the end: the martyrs under the altar cry, “How long, O Lord, holy and true” (Revelation 6:10). The last word is not an explanation but an ending. God will dwell with his people, “‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4), echoing Isaiah 25:8.

keyTexts.why: Pain, toil, and death enter the world after the first sin. The Bible traces suffering to the fall without tying each sorrow to a person's particular sin.
God has seen the affliction of his people, heard their cry, and knows their sufferings, and he comes down to deliver them. The exodus begins with God attending to pain.
Job blesses the name of the LORD after losing everything. The prologue lets the reader know what Job never learns, that his suffering is not punishment.
Job sees God and repents in dust and ashes, and God rebukes the friends who explained his suffering as punishment. The protesting sufferer spoke rightly of God; the explainers did not.
The righteous sufferer cries out that God has forsaken him and does not answer. Jesus takes these words on his lips on the cross.
Amid the ruins of Jerusalem the poet holds grief and hope together: God's mercies are new every morning, and he does not afflict from his heart.
The Servant, a man of sorrows, is pierced for the transgressions of others. Innocent suffering becomes the way God heals and saves.
In darkness Jesus cries the lament of Psalm 22. The Son of God enters the depth of human abandonment rather than explaining it from outside.
Jesus denies that victims of violence and accident were worse sinners than others, and he turns every disaster into a call to repentance for all.
Neither the blind man nor his parents sinned. Jesus rejects the reflex that traces every affliction to a particular sin and points to the works of God.
Present sufferings are real, shared by the whole groaning creation, and not worth comparing with the coming glory and the redemption of the body.
Paul's prayer for relief is answered not with removal but with grace. God's power is made perfect in weakness.
The Son shares flesh and blood, suffers, and is made perfect through suffering, so that he is a merciful high priest able to help those who suffer.
The fiery trial is not strange but a sharing in Christ's sufferings, and those who suffer according to God's will entrust themselves to a faithful Creator.
God will dwell with his people, wipe away every tear, and end death, mourning, crying, and pain. Scripture's final answer to suffering is its abolition.

history:
Jewish readers wrestled with suffering through Job, the Psalms, and the ruin of two temples. The Babylonian Talmud (Berakhot 5a) speaks of ‘sufferings of love’, afflictions that come to the righteous not as punishment but as the loving discipline of Proverbs 3:12. The early church met suffering first as persecution. Ignatius of Antioch, taken to Rome for execution early in the second century, wrote of his longing to imitate the passion of his God, and the account of Polycarp's martyrdom (about 155) praises martyrs who endured but warns against a man who had volunteered himself for arrest and then gave way, because the gospel does not teach people to seek martyrdom. Irenaeus of Lyons (Against Heresies, about 180, book 4) taught that humanity was created immature and meant to grow toward God's likeness through experience of the world, a theme the philosopher John Hick later called the Irenaean type of theodicy (Evil and the God of Love, 1966).

Augustine shaped the Western tradition. Having followed the Manichaeans, who taught that evil is a substance and an eternal power opposed to the good God, he came to hold that evil is not a thing at all but the privation, or lack, of a good that ought to be there (Confessions, book 7, about 400). Evil arises from the misuse of created free will (On Free Choice of the Will), and in the Enchiridion (about 421) he taught that God judged it better to bring good out of evil than to allow no evil to exist. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy (about 524) in prison awaiting execution, and Gregory the Great's great commentary on Job, the Moralia, completed in the 590s, taught the medieval church to read Job as a school of patience. Thomas Aquinas answered the objection from evil against God's existence by citing Augustine's principle (Summa Theologiae I, question 2, article 3). Martin Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (1518) set a theology of the cross, which finds God hidden in suffering and the cross, against a theology of glory, which expects to see God in success and power. The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) begins with the believer's only comfort in life and death and teaches that all things, prosperity and adversity alike, come not by chance but from God's fatherly hand (Questions 1 and 27).

The modern debate took its name from Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, whose Theodicy (1710) argued that God created the best of all possible worlds. The Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755 shook that optimism, and Voltaire mocked it in his poem on the disaster (1756) and in Candide (1759). David Hume's posthumous Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779) pressed the problem against natural theology. In the twentieth century, after two world wars and the Holocaust, many theologians turned to the suffering of God. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, in letters from a Nazi prison in 1944, wrote that only a suffering God can help. Kazoh Kitamori's Theology of the Pain of God (1946) and Jürgen Moltmann's The Crucified God (1972) argued that the cross reveals suffering within God himself, while defenders of classical impassibility such as Thomas Weinandy (Does God Suffer?, 2000) argued that the Son suffers in his human nature and that God's changeless love is the sufferer's surer hope. The church's earlier confession that one of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh (Second Council of Constantinople, 553) stood behind both sides. In philosophy, Alvin Plantinga's free will defense (God, Freedom, and Evil, 1974) answered the claim of J. L. Mackie (1955) that God and evil are logically incompatible, and most philosophers now grant that point while the evidential problem remains debated. C. S. Lewis wrote both a reasoned treatment, The Problem of Pain (1940), and a raw journal of bereavement, A Grief Observed (1961), and many readers have found the second the truer book.

differ.view: Meticulous providence: God ordains suffering for good purposes
differ.body: Augustinian, Thomist, and Reformed Christians hold that nothing, including suffering, falls outside God's decree. God does not do evil, and he is not its author, but he ordains or permits every event for purposes that are good, though often hidden. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20); adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High (Lamentations 3:38); God works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28); and the crucifixion itself was both the crime of wicked men and God's plan (Acts 2:23). Defenders say this is the sufferer's deepest comfort: no pain is random, and none is wasted, even when its reason is never known in this life.

differ.view: Free will: suffering as the cost of real freedom
differ.body: Arminian and Wesleyan Christians, and many others, stress that God made creatures with real freedom and that much suffering comes from its misuse, not from God's will. God permits evil because a world of free persons capable of love is better than a world of automata, and he grieves over what they do (Genesis 6:6). Many connect natural evils to the fall and to creation's bondage to decay (Romans 8:20-21), or to the stable order a world of free agents requires. God does not will each atrocity; he works against it, suffers its effects in Christ, and will redeem it. Defenders say this view keeps God's goodness clear and takes human responsibility seriously.

differ.view: Soul-making: suffering as a school of maturity
differ.body: Drawing on Irenaeus, some theologians stress that God created humanity immature and placed it in a world where virtue, trust, and love can grow through hardship. Scripture speaks of suffering producing endurance, character, and hope (Romans 5:3-4), of trials maturing faith (James 1:2-4), and of God disciplining his children for their good (Hebrews 12:10-11). Defenders do not claim every suffering has a visible lesson; they claim the world as a whole is suited to forming persons who freely come to love God. John Hick gave the view its modern form, though many who use the soul-making theme do not follow his later pluralism.

differ.view: Open theism and spiritual warfare: God at war with evil
differ.body: Some evangelical theologians, notably Gregory Boyd (God at War, 1997; Is God to Blame?, 2003) and John Sanders (The God Who Risks, 1998), argue that the future is partly open because free creatures, human and angelic, really decide it. Much suffering results from the choices of these creatures, including hostile spiritual powers, not from a specific divine purpose. Jesus treated sickness and demonic oppression as enemies to be defeated, not as God's will to be accepted. Defenders say this lets a sufferer know God did not want their child's death and is fighting evil with them. Critics in other traditions judge that the view gives up too much of God's foreknowledge and sovereignty; its defenders reply that it keeps God's love and the reality of the battle.

differ.view: Does God suffer? Impassibility and passibility
differ.body: Classical theology, from the fathers through Aquinas and the Reformers, holds that God is impassible: he is not moved by passions or changed by creatures, and the Son suffered and died in his human nature, so that one of the Trinity truly suffered in the flesh. Defenders say this is good news for sufferers, since a God who is not overwhelmed by suffering can end it, and his love is steady rather than reactive. Passibilist theologians such as Kitamori and Moltmann, and many since, argue that the biblical God grieves (Genesis 6:6), is afflicted in his people's affliction (Isaiah 63:9), and reveals at the cross a suffering love within God himself. The site's page on impassibility sets out this debate in detail.

errors:
The church has rejected the view that every suffering is punishment for the sufferer's particular sin. That was the theology of Job's friends, and God said they had not spoken rightly of him (Job 42:7); Jesus rejected it in John 9 and Luke 13. Its modern form is prosperity teaching, which promises health and wealth to those with enough faith and so implies that the sick and poor lack it. Scripture's great sufferers, Job, Jeremiah, the Servant, Jesus, and Paul with his unremoved thorn, stand against it. The church has also rejected dualism, the Manichaean belief that evil is an eternal power equal to God, and the denial of suffering's reality, whether in ancient docetism, which said Christ only seemed to suffer (the error 1 John 4:2 and Ignatius opposed), or in modern teachings such as Christian Science, which treats sickness and evil as illusions of the mind. Christ's real suffering and real death are part of the church's confession.

Two pastoral distortions are also refused. One treats suffering as good in itself and seeks it; the early church warned against volunteering for martyrdom, Jesus told his disciples to flee persecution when they could (Matthew 10:23), and Paul escaped Damascus in a basket (2 Corinthians 11:33). Texts about enduring unjust suffering (1 Peter 2:19-21) do not require anyone to remain under abuse, and using them that way twists them against the vulnerable they were written to protect. The other is cheap consolation: quoting Romans 8:28 at a graveside, or insisting that grief must be brief. Job's friends did best in their seven days of silence, the Psalms give whole prayers to unrelieved complaint, and Paul tells the church to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15).
life:
The Bible gives sufferers words to pray. Lament is not a failure of faith but one of its forms: telling God the truth, asking how long, and holding him to his promises. The Psalms, Job, Lamentations, and Jesus on the cross show that a person can complain to God and still be his servant. Christians are not promised an explanation for each loss, and they are not asked to call evil good. They are given a God who sees affliction, a Savior who wept and was forsaken, a Spirit who groans with them, and the promise that suffering will not have the last word. That hope does not shorten grief. It lets people grieve, in Paul's phrase, not like those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

The doctrine also shapes how Christians treat those who suffer. The first duty is presence, the seven silent days of Job's friends before they spoke, and practical help, since Jesus healed and fed as well as taught. Those who have been comforted are to comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:4). Suffering can press a person toward despair, and anyone whose pain has turned into thoughts of ending their life should reach out at once to someone who can help: a pastor, a doctor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line such as 988 in the United States. Asking for that help is not a lack of faith. It is one of the ways God keeps his promise not to leave the afflicted alone.
questions: God rebukes Job's friends for their explanations and vindicates Job, who protested. What does that suggest about how Christians should speak to someone who is suffering?

Jesus wept at Lazarus's grave, cried the words of Psalm 22 on the cross, and prayed in Gethsemane for the cup to pass. How does the suffering of Jesus change the way you think about God's relation to your own pain?
Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be removed and was told that God's grace was sufficient. How do you hold together persistent prayer for relief and trust when relief does not come?
